easy.heading: Warming Up With A Simple Grid
easy.body:
Today's easy puzzle was a nice way to wake up my brain. I started by looking at the sum constraint for the three cells at [2,0], [3,0], and [3,1] which had to add up to 3. Since we have a [3,0] domino, I tried placing that at [2,0] and [3,0]. That left just a zero for the cell at [3,1], which fit perfectly with the [3,1] domino being used there and at [3,2].

Next, I looked at the sum of 7 at [2,2] and [2,3]. With the dominoes left, I realized the big [5,5] domino could not fit there, so I used the other pieces to make the equals and sum constraints work. The [0,0] domino went to [0,1] and [1,1], which helped satisfy the sum of 6 when paired with the 5 from the [5,5] piece at [1,2]. It all fell into place once those first few pieces were set.

medium.heading: Getting Into The Groove With Seven Dominoes
medium.body:
The medium puzzle today felt like a little jigsaw. The first thing that caught my eye was the constraint at [0,1] which had to be greater than 4. Looking at my dominoes, like the [4,6] and [6,1], I knew a 6 had to go there. I also saw a sum of 2 at [0,4], which is almost always a 0 and a 2 or two 1s. Since I had a [2,0] domino, that seemed like a great place to start.

What really helped me was the triple equals region at [1,1], [1,2], and [2,1]. Making three different cells have the same number of dots limits your choices a lot. I had to juggle the [6,1] and [6,3] dominoes to make sure the sums and equals matched up. The [2,2] domino was a lifesaver for the sum of 8 at the bottom, helping me balance out the larger numbers from the [6,3] and [4,3] pieces.

hard.heading: Tackling The Big Grid Challenge
hard.body:
The hard puzzle today was a real journey. The biggest challenge was definitely that giant unequal region in the middle where none of the numbers could repeat. I spent a long time just staring at that before I found my way in through the sum of 12 at [3,5] and [4,5]. With dominoes like [6,6], [5,5], and [5,6], there are only a few ways to get a 12, so placing the [6,6] and [5,5] pieces there was my first big breakthrough.

After that, I focused on the equals constraints at the top left. Getting [0,0], [0,1], [1,0], and [2,0] to all match required some careful placement of the smaller dominoes like [1,1] and [0,2]. I almost got stuck at the bottom with the empty cell at [7,0], but then I realized it had to be part of the [6,0] domino. It took a bit of trial and error to make sure the [4,6] and [4,5] pieces did not break the unequal rule in the center, but once those were down, the rest of the grid filled in fast.

explanation.tips: Always start by looking for small sum targets or greater than constraints because they really limit which dominoes you can use. If you see a region where multiple cells must be equal, check your dominoes for doubles or pieces with matching numbers that can sit next to each other. Don't be afraid to place a piece and see if it works, but keep an eye on the remaining numbers so you don't run out of the ones you need for later sums.
explanation.learned: I learned today that the unequal regions are actually easier if you save them for last because the leftover dominoes often only fit one way. I also realized how much a single empty cell can change the whole layout of a corner.

faqs.question: How do you play the NYT Pips puzzle?
faqs.answer: You place standard dominoes onto a grid so that they satisfy mathematical constraints like sums, equality, or inequalities shown in specific regions.

faqs.question: What does the unequal constraint mean in Pips?
faqs.answer: An unequal region means that every single cell inside that highlighted area must contain a different number of pips, with no repeats allowed.

faqs.question: Can you rotate dominoes in the NYT Pips game?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can place dominoes either horizontally or vertically to fit the grid and satisfy the constraints of the puzzle.

faqs.question: What is the best strategy for hard Pips puzzles?
faqs.answer: Look for the most restrictive constraints first, like very high sums or very low sums, and use those to lock in your high-value dominoes like the double six.

faqs.question: Are all dominoes in the list used for the puzzle?
faqs.answer: Yes, to solve the puzzle correctly, you must use every domino provided in the list exactly once to fill the grid.
